Hello, Doctor Nilo, Sofia here from the FIFA Leadership in Football program office. Your module in Miami starts in a few weeks, so here is some practical advice about the local business culture. First, time. Meetings in the United States usually start exactly on time, and many people arrive five minutes early. If you are going to be late, send a short message before the meeting. Second, small talk. Americans are used to short small talk, about two or three minutes, and then they go straight to business. Third, personal space. People usually stand about an arm's length apart, and they do not touch much during a first meeting. A handshake is appropriate; a hug is not. Many of our international participants told me the same thing: at first it felt cold, but they got used to it in a few days. So relax, be punctual, and keep the first conversation short and friendly. See you in Miami.

When I started working with international partners, I made a lot of small mistakes. In Brazil, I used to arrive at meetings ten or fifteen minutes late, and nobody worried about it. I used to spend the first twenty minutes talking about football and family before we discussed any business. My first meeting with an American sponsor was a shock. I arrived ten minutes late, and the director was already looking at his watch. I started to tell a long story about the weekend, and he politely asked to see the agenda. I was not used to that style. On reflection, it was a cultural misunderstanding, not a problem with me. Today, things are different. I am used to arriving early for international meetings, and I keep the small talk short. It took me about a year to get used to it. My advice to colleagues is simple: do not judge the other culture with a stereotype; learn the custom and adapt.
